reasoning_traces.think:
The core innovation lies in representing football as a graph: each player and the ball form a node with 9-dimensional features (position, velocity, etc.), forming a fixed 24-node graph. The GNNs (GCN/GAT) process these features through convolutional or attention mechanisms to produce Q-values for 19 discrete actions. This approach avoids rasterizing spatial data into images, which wastes capacity and slows training compared to CNNs. The DQN framework uses experience replay and target networks to stabilize learning. However, the paper's training setup (batch size 1, gradient clipping 0.7) introduces instability. GATs suffer from collapse on easy and Kaggle scenarios, indicating attention instability. The lack of explicit edge definition and node feature specification limits reproducibility. These primitives enable modeling of spatial and relational dynamics but require careful calibration for NFL applications.
